title: Winter Cycling Nutrition: How to Fuel Your Training Through an Irish Winter
seo_title: Winter Cycling Nutrition: Fuel Your Training in Ireland | Vivify Sports
meta_description: How to fuel winter cycling in Ireland: carbs on cold rides, hydration when you're not thirsty, vitamin D, immunity and turbo sessions. By a sports nutritionist.
excerpt: Cold, wet and dark: an Irish winter changes how you should eat and drink on the bike. Here is how to fuel your base miles, stay healthy and arrive at spring ready to race.

image.alt: Bowl of warm porridge topped with blueberries, seeds and nuts, a winter breakfast for cyclists

body:
Winter is where your next season is built. Long base miles in the cold, wet rides on Irish back roads and indoor sessions on the turbo all put different demands on your body. Many riders keep eating exactly as they do in summer, or cut back hard to lose weight before spring. Both can leave you tired, run down and missing sessions. Here is how I help the cyclists I coach fuel their winter training.

1. Keep fuelling your rides, even the easy ones

Cold weather does not reduce the energy your muscles need. Riding in the cold can even raise energy use a little, especially if you get chilled and start to shiver. Winter base rides are often long, so running low on carbohydrate is a real risk.

As a guide for rides longer than about 90 minutes:

  • 1 to 2.5 hours: around 30 to 60 g of carbohydrate per hour.
  • Longer than 2.5 hours: up to 60 to 90 g per hour, if your gut is trained for it.
  • Easy rides under an hour: a good meal beforehand is usually enough.

Bars and gels harden in the cold, so keep them in an inner pocket close to your body. Real food works well in winter too: rice cakes, banana bread or a jam sandwich are easy to eat with gloves on. If you want to understand carbohydrate targets in more detail, read my guide to how many carbs per hour you need.

2. Drink even when you don't feel thirsty

In the cold, your sense of thirst is blunted, so it is easy to finish a ride dehydrated without noticing. You still lose fluid through sweat under winter layers and through your breathing in cold, dry air.

  • Drink small amounts regularly, for example a few mouthfuls every 15 to 20 minutes.
  • Fill a bottle with warm squash or tea, or use an insulated bottle, so you actually want to drink it.
  • Weigh yourself before and after a long ride: a big drop in weight means you need to drink more next time.

3. Indoor training: you sweat more than you think

On the turbo there is no wind to cool you, so sweat rates can be higher than on the road, even in a cold garage. For indoor sessions of an hour or more, have one or two bottles ready, use a fan, and add electrolytes if you are a salty sweater. Hard interval sessions also run on carbohydrate, so a drink with carbohydrate or a small snack helps you hit your numbers.

4. Look after your immune system

Winter brings colds and flu, and hard training on too little food makes you more likely to pick them up. The basics matter most:

  • Eat enough. Under-fuelling is one of the biggest risks to your health and performance. If you want to lose weight in the off-season, do it slowly and never on your key sessions.
  • Carbohydrate around hard sessions helps limit the stress hormones that can weaken your immune defences.
  • Protein at every meal supports recovery and immune cells: eggs, yogurt, fish, meat, tofu, beans and lentils.
  • Fruit and vegetables every day for vitamins, minerals and fibre.
  • Sleep is part of your nutrition plan: aim for 7 to 9 hours.

5. Vitamin D in Ireland

Between October and March, the sun in Ireland is too weak for your skin to make much vitamin D. Low vitamin D is common in Irish athletes in winter, and it plays a role in bone health, muscle function and immunity. Oily fish, eggs and fortified foods help, but they are often not enough on their own. Speak to your GP or a sports nutritionist about testing your levels and whether a supplement is right for you.

6. Recover with a warm, balanced meal

After a cold ride, a warm meal is what most of us crave, and it is a great opportunity to recover well. Aim for a meal with carbohydrate to refill your energy stores, around 20 to 30 g of protein to repair your muscles, and vegetables. Good options include porridge made with milk and topped with fruit and nuts, a bowl of soup with wholegrain bread and eggs, or a shakshuka with chickpeas and toast. You will find more ideas in my e-book Breakfasts to Ignite Your Potential.

7. Don't forget your iron

Endurance training, heavy sweating and, for women, menstruation all increase iron needs. Low iron makes you feel tired and flat on the bike. Include iron-rich foods such as red meat, beans, lentils, dark green vegetables and fortified cereals, and pair plant sources with vitamin C (for example orange juice or peppers) to absorb more. If you feel unusually tired, ask your GP for a blood test before taking an iron supplement.

Make this winter count

Winter training is a long game. Riders who fuel their rides, stay healthy and recover well are the ones who arrive at spring fitter and ready to race.
